items.title: Sailing along a constant compass bearing draws a spiral around the pole
items.claim: A 'rhumb line' (loxodrome) is a path that crosses every meridian at the same angle — what you sail if you hold a constant compass course. Except for due east/west (the equator) or due north/south, a rhumb line spirals around the pole, eventually reaching it after infinite winding.
items.prompt: Why doesn't a constant bearing give a great circle?

options.text: Great circles change bearing as you traverse them (except along the equator or meridians); to maintain a constant compass bearing, you must follow a different curve that spirals — the loxodrome
It only happens near the pole

items.reveal:
A loxodrome (rhumb line) is the curve that intersects all meridians at the same angle. On a sphere, this is an equiangular spiral.

For any constant bearing not aligned with the equator or a meridian, the path spirals around the pole. The length to reach the pole is finite (the spiral converges) but the number of windings is infinite.

On a Mercator projection, rhumb lines appear as straight lines — this is the property Mercator designed his projection for in 1569. Hold a ruler against a Mercator chart and you have a constant compass bearing course.

Great circles, by contrast, appear as curves on Mercator maps, generally bowed toward the nearer pole. Modern aviation uses great-circle routes; old-school open-ocean sailing used rhumb lines (easier to navigate without constant heading recalculation).

In practice: long-distance navigation often combines them — fly an approximate great circle, but compute waypoints at intervals (e.g., every 5 degrees of longitude) and sail rhumb lines between waypoints. This is 'composite sailing'.

The loxodrome was first studied by the Portuguese navigator Pedro Nunes (1537). It contributed to the systematic mathematisation of navigation in the Age of Discovery.
items.why: Compasses point to magnetic north. Holding a constant bearing draws a curve that no Euclidean intuition prepares you for — and the difference between loxodrome and great circle has shaped maps, navigation, and naval strategy for centuries.

items.title: The set of all sets that don't contain themselves
items.claim: Define R as the set of all sets that don't contain themselves. Does R contain itself? If yes — then by definition it doesn't. If no — then by definition it does. Russell discovered this in 1901 and broke set theory.
items.prompt: How did mathematicians fix the problem?

options.text: By restricting what can be a 'set' — modern Zermelo-Fraenkel axioms (ZFC) only allow forming sets in specific controlled ways (separation, replacement, union, power set), and you can't form 'the set of all sets'
By ignoring sets that contain themselves

items.reveal:
Gottlob Frege spent decades building arithmetic from formal logic. His Grundgesetze (Vol II, 1903) was at the printer when Bertrand Russell wrote to him pointing out the paradox. Frege added a despairing postscript: 'A scientist can hardly meet with anything more undesirable than to have the foundation give way just as the work is finished.'

The paradox: define R = {x : x is not an element of x}. Is R in R?
- If R is in R, then by R's definition R is not in R. Contradiction.
- If R is not in R, then R satisfies the criterion to be in R. Contradiction.

Resolution: in ZFC, the axiom schema of separation only allows forming {x in A : phi(x)} from an EXISTING set A. You can't form 'all sets such that phi'. There is no universal set.

The Barber's paradox (the barber shaves all who don't shave themselves; does he shave himself?) is a pop-culture version.
items.why: Naive set theory looks intuitive — define a set by any property. Russell showed this leads directly to contradiction, and modern set theory had to carefully restrict what counts as a set.

items.title: The most important open problem in mathematics
items.claim: Riemann conjectured in 1859 that all non-trivial zeros of the zeta function lie on the line Re(s) = 1/2. The conjecture controls the distribution of primes among integers. Proving (or disproving) it has been unsolved for 165 years.
items.prompt: Why do we care about complex zeros of a strange function?

options.text: The distribution of prime numbers is encoded in the zeros of the Riemann zeta function — proving the Riemann hypothesis would establish a vast number of theorems in number theory that are currently conditional on it
It tells us the value of zeta at integer points
It's part of the definition of pi

items.reveal:
Riemann's only paper on number theory (1859) defined the analytic continuation of the zeta function and noted that the function has 'trivial zeros' at -2, -4, -6, ... and other 'non-trivial zeros' in the strip 0 less than Re(s) less than 1. He conjectured all non-trivial zeros lie exactly on Re(s) = 1/2.

The Prime Number Theorem (Hadamard, de la Vallée Poussin, 1896) says the count of primes up to x is asymptotically x / ln x. The Riemann hypothesis would tighten the error term enormously.

Thousands of theorems in modern number theory are stated 'assuming RH'. A proof would make them unconditional. Conversely, a disproof would force major rewrites.

The first 10 trillion non-trivial zeros have all been computed and verified to lie on Re(s) = 1/2 (Gourdon, 2004). This doesn't prove the hypothesis.

The Clay Mathematics Institute lists it as one of seven Millennium Prize Problems, with a $1,000,000 reward. So far, only Poincaré (Perelman, 2003) has been solved.
items.why: Primes look like a chaotic distribution. The Riemann hypothesis says they have hidden, beautiful regularity controlled by complex analysis — and 165 years of effort haven't proved or disproved it.
